claims.text: High-pressure torsion processing can improve the hardness and strength of high-entropy alloys without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
The proposed intervention applies to high-entropy alloys in an as-cast or conventionally processed initial state.
High-pressure torsion is the single proposed processing intervention.
HPT at room temperature, 5 GPa, and 5 torsion turns will produce the proposed improvement.
HPT causes grain refinement in the targeted high-entropy alloys.
HPT introduces lattice distortions in the targeted high-entropy alloys.
HPT-induced grain refinement and lattice distortion increase dislocation density and dislocation interactions.
Enhanced dislocation density and interactions increase alloy strength and hardness.
The HPT-treated alloy will have at least 20% greater Vickers hardness than the untreated alloy of the same composition.
The HPT-treated alloy will have at least 15% greater yield strength than the untreated alloy of the same composition.
The predicted hardness and strength gains will occur without a significant reduction in ductility.
The relevant baseline is an untreated high-entropy alloy having the same composition.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for FCC high-entropy alloys.
The hypothesis is expected to hold when the high-entropy alloy contains at least five elements.
The optimal lattice-distortion level and HPT conditions for retaining ductility are uncertain.
Conventional annealing provides a comparison condition that does not introduce significant lattice distortion.
The hypothesis is falsified if the stated hardness and strength improvements are absent or if HPT causes a substantial loss of ductility.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines the baseline as an untreated alloy of the same composition, whereas the experiment specifies conventionally annealed material as the comparator. Annealed material is not necessarily equivalent to the stated untreated baseline.
